summary: This note is a long encyclopedic overview of the sea, covering its definition relative to the ocean, seawater chemistry and salinity, temperature and oxygen, sea level change, waves, tsunamis, surface and deep ocean currents, tides, coastal processes, the carbon cycle, and marine life. It also describes human uses of the sea and the fields that study it, such as oceanography and marine geology. The text is cut off partway through its discussion of marine primary producers.
one_line: An encyclopedic overview of the sea covering its definition, seawater chemistry, currents, tides, waves, coasts, carbon cycle and marine life.
key_facts: A sea is a large body of salty water, and the sea commonly refers to the ocean, the wider body of seawater.
The open ocean has about 35 grams of solids per litre, a salinity of 35 ‰, while the Mediterranean Sea is slightly higher at 38 ‰.
The Dead Sea has 300 grams dissolved solids per litre (300 ‰).
Earth's 1,335,000,000 cubic kilometers of sea contain about 97.2 percent of its known water and cover approximately 71 percent of its surface.
Sea level has been rising at an average rate of about 1.8 millimetres per year for at least the last 100 years.
At the last glacial maximum, some 20,000 years ago, sea level was about 125 metres lower than in present times (2012).
Seawater with a typical salinity of 35 ‰ has a freezing point of about −1.8 °C (28.8 °F).
Seawater had an average pH of about 8.2 over the past 300 million years and is now below 8.1 due to ocean acidification.
The Mariana Trench's deepest point is 10.994 kilometres below the surface of the sea.
Tsunamis in the deep open sea have wavelengths of around 80 to 300 miles and travel at speeds of over 600 miles per hour.
The Moon's mass is some 27 million times smaller than the Sun, but it is 400 times closer to the Earth.
Coral reefs occupy less than 0.1 percent of the world's ocean surface, yet their ecosystems include 25 percent of all marine species.
Coastal habitats extend from the shoreline to the edge of the continental shelf, which occupies only 7 percent of the total ocean area.
The global conveyor belt, or thermohaline circulation, takes about a thousand years to complete its circulation pattern.
The Caspian Sea is the largest endorheic basin, with its main inflow from the River Volga and no outflow.
